# A calm place to write for your Astro site.

Zeku is a native app that opens your Astro project directly, with live-preview markdown, frontmatter that knows your schema, and a publish button.

![The Zeku window: a file tree on the left, a markdown post in live preview in the middle, with its frontmatter above the text](https://zeku.dev/_astro/hero-editor-dark@2x.DLPXFem6_Z8FlqA.webp)![The Zeku window: a file tree on the left, a markdown post in live preview in the middle, with its frontmatter above the text](https://zeku.dev/_astro/hero-editor-light@2x.B9i6oWP-_1BwiLU.webp)

Reads the `content.config.ts` you already have.Edits files in place.Pushes to your repo.

## The one-minute film

[![](https://zeku.dev/_astro/zeku-film-poster.B7QEaUXE_Z11zhEY.jpg)Play the film](https://youtu.be/yk1nQJC_mpg)

Your project

### Opens your repo and reads its schema.

Point Zeku at an Astro project and it finds the content folder on its own. Every collection your `content.config.ts` declares shows up, nested ones included, with field types from the schemas `astro sync` writes.

Nothing is copied into a second config. It is read fresh every time you open the project, so it can never go stale.

- Collections from your config, in the order you think in
- A file tree with Content and Site views
- Any folder of markdown opens too

![The Zeku dashboard showing a Posts collection as cards, with tabs for Pages, Projects, Docs, and Special collections read from the project's config](https://zeku.dev/_astro/dashboard-cards-dark@2x.CakKPEsO_Q4OFB.webp)![The Zeku dashboard showing a Posts collection as cards, with tabs for Pages, Projects, Docs, and Special collections read from the project's config](https://zeku.dev/_astro/dashboard-cards-light@2x.Bo7MQEux_ZE6J3f.webp)

Frontmatter

### Frontmatter that knows your schema.

Zeku draws a form from your collection schema. Enum fields offer their allowed values, `reference()` fields look up entries in the target collection, dates get a picker, booleans get a checkbox, and required fields are marked.

Keys your schema does not know keep working, and dates are written back in the format you choose.

src/content/posts/field-notes.md

```
---
title: Field notes from a slow week
description: What I learned writing every
  morning for a month.
date: 2026-09-18
author: david
category: essays
tags:
  - writing
  - habits
draft: false
---
```

Frontmatter

Writing

### Markdown that renders while you write.

Syntax fades until your cursor reaches it. Callouts, Starlight admonitions, tables, footnotes, math, mermaid diagrams, and Expressive Code blocks render in place.

YouTube, Bluesky, CodePen, and Gist embeds show up inline, and raw HTML renders where it sits. Flip to source any time.

![A post in Zeku's live preview with a rendered callout, a table, and a code block with a title](https://zeku.dev/_astro/live-preview-dark@2x._vqlY-ii_Z2cDni3.webp)![A post in Zeku's live preview with a rendered callout, a table, and a code block with a title](https://zeku.dev/_astro/live-preview-light@2x.BP86anvF_Z1WUmro.webp)

Preview

### See the real site as you write.

Zeku starts your project's own `astro dev`, with whichever of pnpm, npm, yarn, or bun it uses, and shows the page beside the editor.

It renders with your own components, layout, and CSS, so what you see is what ships.

![Zeku with the editor on the left and the live Astro dev server preview of the same page on the right](https://zeku.dev/_astro/site-preview-dark@2x.DOn_TEyg_Z2qkKqP.webp)![Zeku with the editor on the left and the live Astro dev server preview of the same page on the right](https://zeku.dev/_astro/site-preview-light@2x.w4asX9QO_Z1ho5IT.webp)

Publish

### Publish without a terminal.

See what changed, write a commit message, and push. Zeku pulls first so you never clobber work from another machine.

Your host builds the push the way it always has. Zeku never deploys anything itself.

![The Zeku publish dialog listing changed files above a commit message field and a Publish button](https://zeku.dev/_astro/publish-dark@2x.Yj7tx7QU_Z1FdmsE.webp)![The Zeku publish dialog listing changed files above a commit message field and a Publish button](https://zeku.dev/_astro/publish-light@2x.DVXMqY0h_106Hl6.webp)

![The Zeku SEO panel scoring a post on title, description, keyword placement, headings, and alt text](https://zeku.dev/_astro/seo-audit-dark@2x.Dla9wo2b_1bedUz.webp)![The Zeku SEO panel scoring a post on title, description, keyword placement, headings, and alt text](https://zeku.dev/_astro/seo-audit-light@2x.DnudOGvR_Z25HxDj.webp)

SEO

### An audit for every page, and every collection.

Title and description length, keyword placement, heading order, alt text, reading level, and internal links that resolve. Run it on one page with `Ctrl`  `Shift`  `A`, or score a whole collection at once. You set the thresholds.

![A Starlight docs project in Zeku, with pages listed in the same order as the site's sidebar](https://zeku.dev/_astro/starlight-sidebar-dark@2x.Bqq6vAE1_2kt4jD.webp)![A Starlight docs project in Zeku, with pages listed in the same order as the site's sidebar](https://zeku.dev/_astro/starlight-sidebar-light@2x.D61IqwZa_JOAGa.webp)

Starlight

### Docs sites sort like their sidebar.

Starlight projects list pages in the order your sidebar shows them, so the dashboard matches what your readers see.

- ### MDX component builder


Press Ctrl+/ to search your own components, fill in props, pick a hydration directive, and insert. The import is added for you.

- ### Images land in the right place


Drag, drop, or paste and the file is copied into your assets folder with a clean name and a relative link. Stock photo search is built in.

- ### A dashboard per collection


Cards or list, search, tag and draft filters, and bulk actions for publishing, tagging, or setting a frontmatter key on many entries at once.

- ### Theme settings as a form


Themes that mark their options in src/config.ts, like Axis and Astro Modular, get a real settings screen. Everything else opens as source.

- ### Spellcheck that stays local


A bundled English dictionary plus your own word list. It skips code and URLs, and nothing you write leaves your machine to be checked.

- ### Hard to lose work


Autosave, crash recovery kept outside your repo, and a prompt instead of an overwrite when a file changes on disk under you.

- ### Zen mode



[... middle omitted — see footer ...]


If your site uses Astro content collections, yes. Zeku is tested on the 200 most popular Astro themes and the official starters: see [how each one did](https://zeku.dev/themes). Themes that mark their settings in `src/config.ts`, like Axis and Astro Modular, also get a real settings form, and Starlight docs sites sort the way their sidebar does.

Do I have to stop using Obsidian or Vault CMS?

No. Zeku never reads or writes `.obsidian`, so both can point at the same folder and neither rewrites the other. Vault CMS stays free.

How does publishing work?

Zeku uses your own git. It shows what changed, commits with your message, pulls, and pushes. Your host deploys the push the way it always does. Zeku never deploys anything itself.

Is there any AI in it?

No, on purpose. Use whatever AI tools you like for building the site. Zeku is where you write.

Is it on Mac or Linux?

Yes, both in beta. On a Mac, Zeku runs on macOS 10.15 Catalina and later, on Apple Silicon and Intel: run `curl -fsSL https://zeku.dev/install.sh | bash` in Terminal, or download the .dmg from the [download page](https://zeku.dev/download#mac). On Linux, Zeku runs on x86\_64 with glibc 2.35 or later, such as Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Fedora 36 or current Arch: run the same command in a terminal to install it for your account, or download the AppImage, .deb, or .rpm from the [download page](https://zeku.dev/download#linux). The command and the AppImage update themselves; the .deb and .rpm update when you install a newer one. One license covers Zeku on any platform, on up to 3 computers.

Is it a subscription?

No. You pay once, and every update after that is free. After the 14-day trial, Zeku keeps working and reminds you to buy.

## Open your project. Start writing.

Try it free. No account or setup, and nothing added to your repo.

### An app your team will actually enjoy using

A clean, responsive interface that gets out of the way so people can focus on writing.

- Intuitive UI with dark mode, keyboard shortcuts and drag-and-drop uploads
- Instant full-text search across every collection and asset
- Full-fledged asset library with folders, filters and previews
- Spreadsheet-style editing of many entries at once
- Works on phones and tablets, with quick QR code sign-in
- Drafts are backed up automatically, and you’re warned before overwriting someone else’s changes
- Accessible by design, with full keyboard and screen reader support

[See features for editors →](https://sveltiacms.app/en/features/editors)

![A list of blog posts with thumbnails, publish dates, authors and tags](https://sveltiacms.app/images/landing/entry-list-dark.webp?20261015)![A list of blog posts with thumbnails, publish dates, authors and tags](https://sveltiacms.app/images/landing/entry-list-light.webp?20261015)

### One config file, no servers to maintain

Describe your content in a single config file and add a script tag. No backend to host, no database to back up, no upgrades to install.

- Works with Astro, Eleventy, Hugo, Jekyll, Next.js, SvelteKit and any other framework
- GitHub, GitLab, Gitea and Forgejo backends, with OAuth or token sign-in
- Edit a local repository directly in the browser, without a proxy server
- JSON schema validation and autocompletion for your config file
- JavaScript API for custom field types, previews and editor components
- npm package with TypeScript types that loads nothing from third-party CDNs
- Official Agent Skill and llms.txt for AI coding assistants

[See features for developers →](https://sveltiacms.app/en/features/developers)

backend:
  name: github

media_folder: /public/media

collections:

    folder: /content/posts
    fields:
      - { name: title, widget: string }
      - { name: date, widget: datetime }
      - { name: body, widget: richtext }
```

### A website your whole team can keep up to date

Give staff and volunteers an easy way to update your site, with no license fees, no servers to run and an optional review step before changes go live.

- Free and open source forever, with no per-seat or per-site pricing
- Host for free on Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, etc.
- Multilingual sites with one-click AI translation
- Editorial Workflow for reviewing changes before they go live
- Optional built-in image optimizer converts uploads to WebP
- Trusted by government agencies, universities and nonprofits worldwide

I've made a lot of these by hand, and they take far longer than they should. No single part is especially hard, but there are a hundred small decisions and every one of them shows. Stageshow is my attempt to write those decisions down, so an agent can make them too.

* * *

# Getting started

```
npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow
```

That adds the skill for any agent: Grok Build, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, etc. Then ask for something small: one interaction, in one product, at one size.

```
A small looping demo for our homepage hero: someone assigns an issue to a teammate.
```

The agent reads the skill, starts from the closest example, builds the demo, then films it and fixes what it finds. What you get is an ordinary React component, so you can put it anywhere and change it like the rest of your code.

It still may not nail it in one shot. The first pass is usually a big step up from what an agent makes on its own, but most demos still take me a few rounds of feedback.

fair warning

* * *

# What's in it

references/rehearse.md

What the agent works with.

`SKILL.md`

What the agent reads first: the one idea, the five ways faux UI fails, a seven-step workflow, a table of the gold examples, the kit at a glance and a summary of framing.

`references/`

Craft (restraint, type, spacing, colour), motion (story, pace, the cursor), framing (crops, satellites, layouts), grids, looks and backgrounds, annotations, real products and brand marks, filming and the checklist, good and bad pairs side by side, and every kit part's props. Most rules came from reviewing real attempts, and each gives its reason.

`examples/`

Dozens of gold examples the agent starts from and holds its work against, from a hero demo and bento grids to a phone swipe and a dashboard paired with a lock screen.

`kit/`

A small set of React parts the agent can build with, plain code that lives with your demo. It makes the hard parts hold up; it doesn't supply a look. The stage, windows and phones drawn from real geometry, motion that has to survive frame by frame, and a few quiet parts to restyle.

`scripts/`

film.mjs films a demo, lays the frames on a contact sheet and reports what it can measure. jumps.mjs catches one-frame snaps a sheet misses, and layout.mjs checks that text and controls fit their boxes.

* * *

# The playground

The skill also comes with a playground. Run it from the skill's folder:

```
npm install
npm run dev
```

It has every example in the skill, the kit's parts on their own, and a set of comparisons: the same thing done badly and done well, side by side. They're there for the agent as much as for you. "Don't shrink the whole app into a card" is easy to agree with and easy to skip, but much harder to ignore once you see both side by side.

* * *

# What the skill teaches

The skill is built around one sentence:

It reads as a real product, simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion has a cause.

the whole skill, really

Faux UI from agents tends to go wrong in the same few ways. The most common are _too much_ (real words in every cell, packed tight), _too little_ (a wireframe that doesn't read as a product) and _boxed_ (the whole window shrunk into a card, like a pasted screenshot). Then there's _flat_, where everything has the same weight, and _bland_, where the brief's style never shows up.

Here's one demo going from the first to the last, the way the agent builds it: someone assigns a support conversation to Maya.

Correct, but boxed in like a screenshot.The window pins to the corner and runs off the edge, and the one card the story needs slides in over it.Now it plays: the menu opens, Maya is picked, it all resets. With no cursor, it seems to run by itself.A cursor gives each change a cause, except the last, where Maya vanishes with nothing there to undo her.The avatar flies to its row and holds, then the cursor undoes it on screen, so the loop has no visible seam.

Left to itself, an agent drifts toward the first. It knows what a support inbox contains, so it fills every row. The skill has it keep only the words the story needs and use placeholder lines for the rest, so the inbox still looks full without asking you to read it. It also decides the crop first, so it doesn't waste time building things nobody will see.

* * *

# How a demo is built

Every demo is a stage: a canvas with a design size. Its contents are drawn from state, and a script changes that state one beat at a time. The cursor is part of the stage, and it aims at things by name.

```
async function script(a: Act<S>) {
  await a.click({ at: "share" }); // arcs there, presses
  await a.set({ open: true }); // resolves once painted
  await a.wait(2000); // the payoff holds

Parts stay mounted while they transition, so they can move in and out instead of popping. Positions are measured, so the cursor lands in the right place and overlays line up at any size. And the kit handles the motion that's hard to get right by hand, like a number that rolls only the digits that changed, a card flying into a slot, or a message forming out of the text field.

There's also a camera, so a stage can push in on the important bit and pull back out. It sits on top of the scene, so you don't have to change the scene to use it.

Most of the rules started as a note on a real demo, like "the shadow is too harsh" or "this title isn't centred." Once a note is in the skill, every demo after it gets it for free. You can do the same: when you correct a demo, ask the agent to add the note to the skill.

Model taste is getting better with every release, and I suspect a skill like this is only useful for a while, since much of what it teaches and includes could soon come built in.

Some of it already has. Early on in making this, the references had rules a newer model simply didn't need, like keeping the traffic lights the right size, and as the models improved those rules quietly stopped doing anything.

Others have held up across every model I've tried, mostly the ones about framing and motion. Models are perfectly capable of getting those right, but they don't seem to know that they matter until something tells them.

Until then, it helps, and every demo made with it is a small, well-built example of this kind of UI, which is the sort of thing models learn from. If it plays a small part in making itself unnecessary, that's fine by me.

[Start trial](https://account.sitereal.app/start?plan=trial) [Read the docs](https://sitereal.app/docs) Presentation of the sitereal app and its functionalities. The builder ## Draw the page on a canvas that edits files. Every breakpoint at once, a tree carrying your own class names, and a Style panel writing into the one rule that actually styles the element. Select a heading and .hero\_\_title opens — not a copy of it. [Explore the builder](https://sitereal.app/builder) Features ## Everything your site needs, built into sitereal. ### Design Compose responsive pages on a visual canvas. ### Code Edit the real files, here or in your editor. ### Agents Let Claude Code build and maintain pages. ### MCP Connect any MCP client to the open project. ### Reuse Components, templates, snippets and presets. ### Design system Eighteen modules of tokens you can switch off. ### Content One schema gives you types, forms and queries. ### Motion Reveals and scroll links, as plain attributes. ### SEO Titles, structured data, sitemap and robots. ### Ship Its own git repository. Hosts anywhere. Real code ## Paste HTML, get a tree. Read the tree, get the HTML back. Same class names, no builder-owned wrapper, and no generated name you did not choose. LayerOutput 1 2 3Pricing 4 5 6Yearly 7€69

8 9 10 11 Format HTML ⇄ LayerOutput Search… sectionPricing divContainer h2Title divGrid articleCard h3Name pPrice Workflow ## Three moves, and the third one is git push. There is no publish button that phones home, because there is nothing to phone — branches, pull and push are plain git against your own remote. 1. Step 01 ### Open a folder Point sitereal at an Astro project you already have, or scaffold a new one. It gets its own git repository at once — a site’s history has nothing to do with the tool that drew it. 2. Step 02 ### Compose Sections, containers, elements. Style through the token layer or write the CSS yourself in the same panel: the two are views of one stylesheet, not a round trip. 3. Step 03 ### Commit Save, and real files land under src/. Push them. Deploy to Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare, a bucket or your own box. Nothing on that server has ever heard of sitereal. main Branches main pricing-page docs/rewrite new-branch-name Origin origin/main · 2 commits behind Pull from GitHub Commit Pricing page, second pass Commit all changes (7) GitHub meinaufwind/sitereal · 3 to push Commit & push to origin/main ### Branches Every branch the repository has, local and on origin, and a field that starts a new one. Switching keeps unfinished work with the branch it belongs to and hands it back when you return, instead of dragging it onto another one. ### Pull Fetch and rebase onto origin, autostashed, so whatever you were in the middle of survives it. On a conflict git stops and you are handed its own message, not a summary of it. ### Push Stage, commit and push to origin, in one press. Nothing is ever committed or pushed on your behalf — the engine runs git when you ask it to and at no other moment. Hosting ## A folder of finished pages. Nothing to attack, nothing to wait for. sitereal builds an Astro site, so what you upload is HTML, CSS and images. No PHP on the host, no admin login on the public site, no plugin surface and no database unless you asked for one — and because every page was rendered before anyone asked for it, there is nothing left to compute while a visitor waits. ### Nothing on the host to break into A static site is files being served. There is no wp-admin, no plugin with a CVE in it, no database credentials sitting on the machine. The builder runs on your own computer and is never part of the deployed site, so the attack surface a CMS gives away for free simply is not there — and a form's delivery keys stay in environment variables on your host, never in the page. ### Zero JavaScript until you ask for some Astro renders your components at build time and ships no framework runtime by default. Interactivity is an island, loaded only where you place one, and sitereal's own runtimes — motion, navigation, forms, overlays — are a few kilobytes each and emitted only for the pages that actually use them. ### The page is finished before the request arrives Every route is built once and served as a file, from a CDN, an object store or the cPanel plan a client already pays for. Nothing renders per visit, so there is no cache plugin to invalidate, no page that gets slower under load, and hosting costs what static hosting costs. Publish ## One button puts it online. From your computer to your host. Publish builds the site on your machine and uploads it to Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare or the web hosting a client already has — no repository, no build settings on the host, and only the files that changed. [How publishing works](https://sitereal.app/docs/publishing). ### Your host, your account Sign in with Netlify or Cloudflare, paste a Vercel token, or enter any FTP or SSH login. Tokens stay in your computer’s keychain, and the site goes straight to the host — never through us. ### Preview first, roll back after A preview link to send before anything goes live, the recent publishes listed, and any of them put back in one click. ### GitHub still works beside it Push to GitHub and let a host build from the repository, publish directly, or both. The site is plain Astro, so moving to another host later changes nothing in it. Questions ## Answered plainly. If something here is still unclear, the documentation goes considerably deeper. [Read the docs](https://sitereal.app/docs) ### What does it cost? Seven days free with every feature, then €69 a year — or €199 once. The two licenses give you the same application and differ only in how long they run: the lifetime license never ends, and a yearly license runs for as long as you renew it. When it ends, sitereal stops opening projects until you renew — your sites are ordinary files and keep building without it. Full details are on the pricing page. ### What exactly does it write into my project? src/pages/.astro for each page, src/components/.astro for each component, src/layouts/Layout.astro for each template, the generated stylesheets under src/styles/generated/, the small runtimes under public/scripts/, and your content and media as ordinary files. One extra file, site.sitereal, holds what the canvas knows — and the site never reads it. ### Can I hand-edit the code afterwards? Yes, and that is the point: visual editing and hand-editing are two views of the same files. Change a page, a component, a layout or a stylesheet in your editor — or let Claude Code do it — and sitereal reads it back onto the canvas. Or edit them inside sitereal: code mode puts the files beside the canvas. Nothing you write is ever written over — when the canvas changed the same file, the two are merged. ### Does it work with an existing Astro site? Yes. Point it at the folder. It adds its own files and leaves yours alone; a page you wrote by hand shows up in the page list and opens on the canvas as it is, with nothing put around it, and the ones you draw appear alongside it. ### Which platforms does it run on? macOS, Windows and Linux. It is a desktop application — signed and notarized on the Mac, signed on Windows — and the same builder runs in your browser from the sitereal command. Each project runs its own local engine. Downloads are on the download page. ### Can I use it for client work? Yes, on either license, with no separate commercial tier. The sites you build are yours and your clients', with no attribution required and nothing of ours left running in them. ## Start building the sites you’ve always wanted. Seven days free, on your machine — and every site you build is real Astro in your own repository, yours from the first save. [Start the free trial](https://account.sitereal.app/start?plan=trial) [See pricing](https://sitereal.app/pricing) [Download the app](https://sitereal.app/download) ## Cookies on this site We use cookies to run this site and, with your permission, to understand how it is used. ## Is Pages CMS free?

Yes, Pages CMS is 100% free, whether you want to use [the online version](https://app.pagescms.org/), deploy it for free on [Vercel](https://vercel.com/), or self-host it. It's MIT licensed through and through, feel free to extend it as you see fit.

## Do you only support GitHub?

Yes. Supposedly, we could add GitLab and Bitbucket support, but the assumption is the vast majority of users will be on GitHub. Pull requests and issues are welcome: [github.com/pages-cms/pages-cms](https://github.com/pages-cms/pages-cms).

## Why yet another CMS?

I hear you, but I needed Pages CMS to exist. I love static site generators, and while YAML front matter and Markdown aren't terribly complicated, editing content and uploading images using [GitHub.com](http://github.com/) or Git isn't really user-friendly, especially if you're updating the site with a whole team. For that reason, a lot of teams use a headless CMS like Contentful, Sanity, or Strapi. That works, but it's one more dependency and is overkill in most cases. You could also use something like Decap CMS (formerly Netlify CMS). Really cool project, but I've never been a fan of the user experience. And most importantly, I wanted something as simple as possible. Back in 2018, I had built a lightweight CMS ( [Jekyll+](https://github.com/hunvreus/jekyllplus)) with the idea of getting the CMS set up with a single configuration file. Pages CMS is the next iteration of that idea.

## Who built this?

My name is [Ronan Berder](https://ronanberder.com/) ( [@hunvreus](https://x.com/hunvreus)). I live in Singapore. I went back to writing software [after years of building (and ultimately selling) a consultancy in China](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SEzXTXo1D8I).

## I have a problem, how can I get help?

First, make sure to check the [documentation](https://pagescms.org/docs). You can also [ask for help in the Discord channel](https://pagescms.org/chat). Otherwise, [post your issue on GitHub](https://github.com/pages-cms/pages-cms).

- [Star the project on GitHub](https://github.com/pages-cms/pages-cms)
- [Report issues](https://github.com/pages-cms/pages-cms/issues)
- [Send pull requests](https://github.com/pages-cms/pages-cms/pulls)
- [Join the Discord chat](https://pagescms.org/chat)

Is the AI local today?

Not yet. The agent calls the provider you connect: Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter, on your own key. Everything else is already local. The app, your files, your edits and the design work all run on your Mac or Windows PC. No server of ours sits between you and the model. On Splitleaf's server in the EU, encrypted, for that one site. A key is never written to your site folder, so it never ends up in your repository.

The app you bought keeps working and keeps publishing. The licence includes 12 months of updates. A future major version is an optional paid upgrade.

- [Cinder K1](/hero/cinder-k1)
A cinematic mechanical-keyboard hero with a pointer-guided lamp, responsive camera orbit, live keypress feedback, ember particles, firelit typography, and tactile pre-order controls.
- [Velara Vortex](/hero/velara-vortex)
A full-screen brand-and-motion studio hero pairing precise editorial typography with a layered ring of 12 image cards that follows an authored vortex sequence and leans into pointer engagement.
- [Tideform](/hero/tideform-page)
A complete studio hero with a radial phase-field lattice, pointer-warmed crests, click-triggered ignition rings, character-level heading reactions, and restrained editorial navigation.
- [Emberline](/hero/emberline-page)
A complete GPU orchestration hero with glass navigation, restrained editorial copy, social proof, stat cards, and a pointer-reactive blue-white vortex line field.
- [Volta Atelier](/hero/volta-atelier)
The isolated Volta Atelier opening section: an oversized typographic frame around an eleven-card, pointer-reactive studio collage with ambient dust and producer details.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a Three.js hero section?

It is the opening section of a website with an interactive Three.js, WebGL, or shader-driven visual combined with real interface content and calls to action.

### Can I use only the 3D background from a hero?

Many heroes separate the visual scene from the surrounding interface. Check the component source and variants to see whether the background can be reused on its own.

### How do I keep a Three.js hero fast?

Control pixel ratio, geometry and particle counts, pause work when the scene is off-screen, and provide a reduced-motion or static fallback for constrained devices.

### Can the hero match an existing brand system?

Yes. The source can be adapted to your typography, colors, spacing, copy, assets, lighting, camera, and motion while preserving the core interaction.

results.content:
# Anti-Patterns

 57 named patterns across 10 categories. Deceptive design, addictive mechanics, accessibility weaponization, and common UX failures. Each one identified, categorized, and rated.

| Pattern | Severity | Description | Category |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bait and Switch | Critical | Offers one thing, delivers another. User clicks expecting X, gets Y. | Deceptive Patterns |
| Trick Questions | Critical | Uses double negatives, confusing phrasing, or inverted logic so users select the opposite of their intent. | Deceptive Patterns |
| Visual Misdirection | High | Uses size, color, contrast, or positioning to make the business-preferred option look like the only option or the default. | Deceptive Patterns |
| Disguised Ads | High | Makes advertisements look like content, navigation, or system UI. | Deceptive Patterns |
| Hidden Costs | Critical | Reveals fees, taxes, or charges only at the final step of a purchase flow. | Deceptive Patterns |
| Sneak into Basket | Critical | Adds items, insurance, warranties, or donations to a cart without explicit user action. | Deceptive Patterns |
| Confirmshaming | High | Uses guilt, shame, or social pressure in opt-out copy ("No thanks, I don't want to save money"). | Deceptive Patterns |
| Prechecked Consent | Critical | Pre-selects checkboxes for marketing, data sharing, or terms the user hasn't reviewed. | Prechecked & Default Manipulation |
| Opt-Out Burden | Critical | Makes opting out require significantly more effort than opting in (multi-page flows, phone calls, postal mail). | Prechecked & Default Manipulation |
| Privacy Zuckering | High | Defaults to maximum data exposure, relying on users not changing settings. Named after Facebook's repeated defaults. | Prechecked & Default Manipulation |
| Forced Continuity | Critical | Auto-enrolls users in paid subscriptions after free trials without clear warning or easy cancellation. | Prechecked & Default Manipulation |
| Default to Most Expensive | Medium | Pre-selects the highest-cost tier or option in pricing selectors. | Prechecked & Default Manipulation |
| Fake Countdown Timers | Critical | Displays timers that reset, have no real deadline, or create false urgency. | Urgency & Scarcity Fabrication |
| Fabricated Scarcity | Critical | Claims limited availability ("Only 2 left!") that doesn't reflect actual inventory. | Urgency & Scarcity Fabrication |
| Fake Social Proof | Critical | Displays fabricated activity notifications ("15 people viewing this now") or fake reviews. | Urgency & Scarcity Fabrication |
| Pressure Selling | High | Uses time-limited "exclusive" offers designed to prevent comparison shopping. | Urgency & Scarcity Fabrication |
| Loss Framing | Medium | Frames choices as losses ("You're losing $50/month by not upgrading") rather than gains, to exploit loss aversion. | Urgency & Scarcity Fabrication |
| Infinite Scroll | Medium | Removes natural stopping points to maximize session length. No pagination, no "end," no sense of completion. | Addictive Design |
| Variable Ratio Reinforcement | High | Uses unpredictable rewards (likes, notifications, content) to trigger dopamine-driven checking behavior. Slot machine mechanics. | Addictive Design |
| Streak Manipulation | High | Creates artificial loss consequences for missing daily engagement ("Your 30-day streak will be lost!"). | Addictive Design |
| Pull-to-Refresh Gambling | Medium | Makes content refresh feel like pulling a slot machine lever — will there be something new? | Addictive Design |
| Autoplay Chains | Medium | Automatically starts next content without consent, exploiting inertia to extend sessions. | Addictive Design |
| Artificial Incompleteness | Medium | Shows progress bars or "profile completeness" scores that exploit completion bias to extract more data or engagement. | Addictive Design |
| Permission Harassment | High | Repeatedly asks for permissions (notifications, location, contacts) after user has declined. | Attention Exploitation |
| Notification Spam | High | Sends excessive, low-value notifications to pull users back into the product. | Attention Exploitation |
| Obstruction Interstitials | High | Blocks content with full-screen overlays, newsletter signups, or app-install prompts that are difficult to dismiss. | Attention Exploitation |
| Attention Bait | Medium | Uses misleading notification badges, unread counts, or red dots to manufacture urgency. | Attention Exploitation |
| Nagging | Medium | Persistent prompts to rate, review, share, upgrade, or complete actions the user has shown no interest in. | Attention Exploitation |
| Inaccessible Unsubscribe | Critical | Makes cancellation or opt-out flows fail with screen readers, keyboard navigation, or other assistive tools. | Accessibility Weaponized |
| CAPTCHA as Gatekeeping | High | Uses CAPTCHA challenges that are disproportionately difficult for users with disabilities, without providing accessible alternatives. | Accessibility Weaponized |
| Low-Contrast Opt-Out | High | Makes opt-out links or decline buttons deliberately low-contrast, tiny, or visually suppressed. | Accessibility Weaponized |
| Assistive Technology Traps | Critical | Creates keyboard focus traps or reading-order manipulation that confuses assistive tech in the area of consent or cancellation flows. | Accessibility Weaponized |
| Child-Targeted Manipulation | Critical | Uses game-like mechanics, character appeals, or peer pressure to drive purchases or data collection from children. | Vulnerable User Exploitation |
| Elderly-Targeted Confusion | Critical | Exploits lower digital literacy with complex flows, jargon-heavy interfaces, or hidden cancellation paths. | Vulnerable User Exploitation |
| Crisis Exploitation | Critical | Takes advantage of users in urgent situations (medical, financial, legal) with high-pressure tactics or inflated pricing. | Vulnerable User Exploitation |
| Addiction Exploitation | Critical | Targets users with known addictive behaviors (gambling, shopping, social media) with triggering mechanics. | Vulnerable User Exploitation |
| Financial Vulnerability Targeting | Critical | Offers predatory financial products with deliberately obscured terms to users showing financial stress signals. | Vulnerable User Exploitation |
| Anthropomorphic Manipulation | High | Gives AI human-like emotional responses to make users feel guilt, attachment, or obligation toward the system. | AI-Specific Dark Patterns |
| Opaque Personalization | High | Uses recommendation algorithms to create filter bubbles or steer choices without the user understanding why they see what they see. | AI-Specific Dark Patterns |
| Manufactured Dependency | High | Designs AI assistance to reduce user competence over time, making them dependent on the tool. | AI-Specific Dark Patterns |
| Simulated Understanding | Medium | Makes AI appear to understand context, emotion, or intent it cannot actually process, creating false trust. | AI-Specific Dark Patterns |
| Algorithmic Exploitation | Critical | Uses behavioral data to identify and exploit individual psychological vulnerabilities at scale. | AI-Specific Dark Patterns |
| Undisclosed AI Decisions | High | Hides the fact that an AI is making consequential decisions (pricing, eligibility, content ranking) from the user. | AI-Specific Dark Patterns |
| Dead Ends | Medium | Flows that terminate without guidance — empty states with no actions, error pages with no recovery path. | Common UX Failures |

[... middle omitted — see footer ...]

| Destructive Defaults | High | Irreversible actions (delete, publish, send) that are too easy to trigger accidentally. | Common UX Failures |
| Broken Error Recovery | High | Error messages that don't explain what went wrong or how to fix it. "An error occurred." | Common UX Failures |
| Assumption of Context | Medium | Expects the user to remember information from previous screens, sessions, or channels. | Common UX Failures |
| Mobile Afterthought | High | Desktop-first design that becomes cramped, broken, or missing features on mobile. | Common UX Failures |
| Real Estate Tour | Medium | Design documentation or rationale that describes what's on screen ("there's a button in the top left with rounded corners") instead of explaining why it's there and what problem it solves. Inventory masquerading as intent. | Common UX Failures |
| Smoothed-arc Personas | High | Constructs a single user narrative arc that smooths over real variance in research. The persona reads coherently when the underlying data showed three or more distinct, non-converging user paths. The team empathizes with a fictional composite, not actual users. | Narrative Pathologies in Design Process |
| Manufactured-Tension Briefs | High | Strategic narratives whose complication is sized to fit a predetermined resolution rather than what evidence shows. Symptom: the tension feels conveniently shaped. Result: teams commit to strategies built on inflated or invented problems. | Narrative Pathologies in Design Process |
| Conflict-Default Journeys | Medium | Frames every user experience as a hero's journey with a goal, obstacle, and resolution — even when the actual experience is habit-shaped, ambient, or recurring. Forces conflict structure onto experiences that don't have it, distorting the design. | Narrative Pathologies in Design Process |
| Story-as-Evidence Substitution | High | Uses narrative emotional appeal to win stakeholder assent for design decisions that aren't supported by research. The story carries the conviction; the evidence is post-hoc or absent. | Narrative Pathologies in Design Process |
| Choreography Role-Reduction | Medium | Service blueprints that flatten humans into system roles. The blueprint reads cleanly because nobody is in it — the customer, the agent, the system are all abstractions. Coordination clarity purchased by erasing the people the service exists for. | Narrative Pathologies in Design Process |
